strategies.name: break_and_retest
strategies.definition: A break and retest is pretty simple. Price breaks above a key level or breaks below a key level, it comes back, it retests that level, and it holds it, and it continues in the original direction. So that level that it breaks is either then becoming support or resistance.

entry_sequence.action: You want to identify your key level. Again, pre-market highs, pre-market lows, the 30-minute opening range high and low, previous day's highs, previous day's lows, a strong area of support or resistance. Now, keep in mind that not all levels matter in the market, but we mainly want to focus on the most obvious ones.

We want to wait for price to break the key level. So, we want strong momentum either at the breakout above resistance or the break below the support level. Now, on top of that, we do want to see volume confirmation. If we break out or if we react off a low volume, it's typically not going to work out. It has to be very quick and aggressive through it, not just like, you know, kind of chopping through it. Literally like a couple big candles through the level, that's what we want to look for. So, if it looks weak, we ignore the setup, and we do not take it.

We want to wait for the retest. We want to wait for price to pull back, price pulls back, tests the level. We want to see price hold the level. If it's able to hold the level, we are then going to look for either bullish price action, if we're looking for price to go up, or bearish price action, if we're looking for price to go down.

I enter after confirmation. So, again, if we do not get confirmation, we do not take the trade. For a long: we want to see bullish price action. Long lower wicks, bullish hammers, dragonfly dojis, etc. That would help confirm to us that this resistance is now becoming support. For a short: we're looking for bearish price action. Long upper wicks, bearish hammers, gravestone dojis, etc. That would help confirm that this trade is truly valid.

direction_entries.long: Price breaks above it, we then want to see price come back down and test it as support. If it can do that, that would be considered a break and retest, and we would be looking to go long to capture a move higher.
direction_entries.short: Price ends up breaking below the support, well now we have the break, we're waiting for price to come back up and retest it as resistance. If it can become resistance, we're looking to go short.

confluences.description: We do want to see volume confirmation. If we break out or if we react off a low volume, it's typically not going to work out.

If you like to use order flow, you could use Bookmap liquidity. So, visually seen on the heat map that buyers or sellers are present at that area. All those things combined, the volume confirmation, the price action telling you to get in, as well as the liquidity on Bookmap, all of that sets up for a very high probability trade.
The first retest is always the highest probability. So don't be sitting there trying to trade every break and retest.
You risk a fixed amount per trade, and you only take A+ setups. One to two trades a day at max.

variants.description: Moving-average reclaim confirmation at the retest: price retests the 80 MA, reclaims it, get back up above that 8 EMA. That's when I went long.
variants.note: Stated only within chart walk-through examples, not as a general rule.

variants.description: Timeframe: setup executed on the 5-minute chart (you go short at the close of this 5-minute candle), with a lower 2-minute timeframe used to refine some entries (maybe it looked better on the 2-minute time frame).
variants.note: Stated only within chart walk-through examples.

stop.description: Your stop is if price breaks back on the opposite side of the breakout level. For longs, right below the break area; for shorts, if price comes back up above the break area. That's it. So, you're not risking a lot when you take these trades.

targets.description: Your target is going to be the next obvious area of liquidity, so could be the previous high or the previous low. Maybe you have a supply zone, demand zone, whatever, but you're targeting clear areas of where liquidity is sitting within the market.

instrument_classification.rationale: The strategy is generic price-action (break and retest of key levels) and is not tied to a specific instrument. All chart walk-throughs are demonstrated on NASDAQ futures ('Let's do this on the NASDAQ futures'), but the mechanic applies to any instrument with identifiable key levels.

coaching_notes: Most traders, they try to predict where price is going. I personally do not. I wait for price to show me where it wants to go, then I enter on confirmation. That's the difference between me and other traders, a profitable trader versus an unprofitable trader.
Step number three, we want to wait for the retest, and this is where most traders mess up. They chase the breakout, but instead, what I do is I wait.
Now, this setup is very powerful, but only if you manage risk correctly.
Again, I always stress this. One to two trades a day, that's it. And this is how I turn consistency into profits.
Now, here's why most people fail this setup. They chase the breakout, they don't wait for confirmation, they trade weak levels, and they overtrade every small move.
This setup, it's very simple, but it requires patience.
So don't be sitting there trying to trade every break and retest.
So if you can master this one setup, you don't need anything else. One clean break, one clean retest, and one execution. That's it. And that's how you stay consistent in trading.
